notes.title: Finally, a two-player online battle mode has been initially realized! ! !
notes.content: [p]Asymmetric online battles can add to the fun of the game, so they're definitely worth developing.[/p][p]The online framework overlaps with the single-player framework, so it's best to initially build the online framework first to avoid overloading the single-player mode with development, which would require extensive modifications later. Currently, we've developed a preliminary online mode, and while it's not perfect, it provides a good starting point. We'll also pay attention to the overall architecture when developing the single-player mode![/p][p]In the two-player online battle mode, the player still plays a tank, as shown in the following diagram:[img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45556920/2ac2bade72f7e2999669aea82505b70e6ebf5687.png"][/img][/p][p][/p][p]You can see that a normal map has been added to the ground to make it less flat. The horse's texture has also been updated to make the color less abrupt. Further polishing will be done later.[/p][p]The opposing team is in infantry formation, as shown below:[/p][p][/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45556920/d0101e2710de13ed5306c1fb69a943e19e61faf5.png"][/img][/p][p]The layout of the formation is still determined by the player on the formation page, as shown below:[/p][p][/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45556920/8c4c01122e230b145e911cd75deb5b352a307ef9.png"][/img][/p][p]There are a total of 100 soldiers, 5 chessmen, 15 shieldmen, 20 spearmen, 30 short swordmen, and 30 archers. Players can arrange the formation freely, but once the formation is set, subsequent soldiers can only move between the infantry positions of the initial layout, as shown in the figure below:[/p][p][img src="{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45556920/d09be9cc9d07f9ddf42ae9b8857b7d77f3ee9a23.png"][/img][/p][p]Initially, since there are no empty spaces within the formation, there's no need to manipulate soldiers' positions. Simply move the entire formation up, down, left, and right to avoid or approach the chariot. Once a soldier dies, the space becomes vacant, allowing you to adjust the soldiers' positions within the formation. For example, you can place the injured soldier in the center of the formation, or shrink the formation to keep the soldiers more concentrated. The more soldiers killed on the infantry side, the more room there is for formation adjustments.[/p][p]Why this design? Primarily to reduce the difficulty of controlling the game.[/p][p]The chariot side only needs to control up, down, left, and right to approach the enemy, automatically attacking them. The player simply controls their rhythm and positioning.[/p][p]The infantry side, on the other hand, only needs to control the entire formation to approach or avoid the chariot. Players must consider their initial formation layout at the beginning. This layout determines the fixed positions of the soldiers throughout the game, so it's important to plan this before the battle. During the battle, since the positions are fixed, there's no need to worry about this; you only need to focus on how to move the individual soldiers.[/p][p]Friends who have played games like Warcraft or StarCraft know that these games are difficult to control because they allow players to freely control the movement and positioning of soldiers, which makes them difficult for novice players. We hope that the games we develop will be relatively simple and easy to control, which may bring more different experiences.[/p][p][/p][p][/p][p][/p][p][/p]

notes.title: Why is my independent game named DaiConflict: Jia vs. Li?
notes.content: [p]At the end of the Warring States period, even after Qin captured the Zhao capital Handan and took King Qian of Zhao hostage, the state of Zhao did not immediately perish. Hundreds of members of the Zhao royal clan followed Prince Jia in fleeing to the Dai region, where he proclaimed himself King of Dai and continued resisting Qin rule for another six years.[/p][p]This episode—briefly mentioned in historical records—has long gone unnoticed by later generations, yet it deeply captured my attention.[/p][p]Prince Jia was originally the crown prince of Zhao, eldest son of King Daoxiang and elder brother of King Qian. However, due to the king’s favoritism toward a consort, Jia was deposed in favor of his younger brother. Thus, he fell from grace.[/p][p]Prince Jia’s life reminds me of Faramir from [i]The Lord of the Rings[/i]—the noble but overlooked son of Denethor II—as well as Fusu, the eldest son of Qin Shi Huang. All were underappreciated by their fathers but proved virtuous and capable in their own right.[/p][p]Few can truly imagine the plight of the Zhao people during those six years resisting Qin in Dai, from 227 to 222 BCE. Just 33 years earlier, in 260 BCE, Zhao had suffered a catastrophic defeat at Changping, where Qin forces slaughtered 450,000 of its soldiers. Considering Zhao’s entire population may have been just around 3 million, the scale of this loss was devastating. Imagine how many families lost fathers, sons, husbands.[/p][p]Zhao's resentment toward Qin ran unimaginably deep.[/p][p]After the fall of their state, many Zhao people refused to surrender. Their hatred for Qin was no less intense than the feelings modern people might have toward historical invaders. Yet Zhao, gravely weakened by the Changping disaster, could not withstand Qin's advance. With Handan lost and their king captured, the people who fled to Dai were not only unable to avenge their losses but also faced utter despair, on the verge of total destruction.[/p][p]Such was the context of suffering and defiance that gave rise to [i]Jia & Li: The Battle at Dai[/i], and the story of Prince Jia.[/p][p]However, portraying only the Zhao people’s despair would be too bleak—so I introduced another key character: Prince Li.[/p][p]Prince Li was originally a fictional character I created—a Zhao aristocrat and childhood friend of Prince Jia. Inspired by Confucius, he traveled across states and witnessed endless war and destruction. Disillusioned by chaos, he defected to Qin, believing it the only power capable of unifying the realm. Eventually, he joins the Qin army and confronts his old friend at Dai.[/p][p]As children, Jia dreamed of being a wise ruler, and Li a virtuous advisor. They pledged to restore Zhao to its former glory, like under King Wuling. But as adults, diverging experiences led them down opposing paths: one refused to surrender, clinging to ideals; the other pursued peace through unification. Who can say who was right?[/p][p]Their story fits Wang Guowei’s third category of tragedy—neither born of villainy (like [i]Hamlet[/i]), nor of blind fate (like [i]Romeo and Juliet[/i]), but of human bonds and circumstances. These are tragic outcomes born from ordinary people in extraordinary situations. Each recognizes the harm yet presses forward, unwilling to back down.[/p][p]All of us, in growing up, have experienced this—childhood companions who grow distant, not from betrayal, but from the inevitable divergence of lives. Like Lu Xun’s [i]Runtu[/i] and [i]Xun-ge[/i].[/p][p]Later, while researching historical texts, I discovered that modeling Prince Li after Li Mu’s real son made the character more resonant. Historical records mention Li Mu had three sons—Li Mi, Li Hong, and Li Xian. Li Mi served Qin and fathered Li Zuoche, a notable strategist during the Qin-Han transition. Given the sparse historical records on Li Mi, he offered rich narrative space.[/p][p]So I reimagined Prince Li as Li Mi, styled Zili—the son of the great Zhao general Li Mu. Though he carried the burden of national enmity, he defected to Qin. His motivations are thus more plausible and compelling.[/p][p]Tragically, Li Mu himself was executed by the Zhao king after Qin’s successful use of deception—perhaps one of China’s earliest “tearing down our own wall” moments. This cycle of wrongly punished patriots has recurred through history—Yue Fei, Yu Qian, Yuan Chonghuan—all echoing that same sorrow.[/p][p]One reason such tragedies repeat is that their stories aren’t remembered deeply enough. I hope my game doesn’t just entertain players but also sparks reflection on history. Even if only a small portion of players pause to think—just a sliver—it would give meaning to all my efforts as a developer.[/p][p]This is a broad overview of [i]Jia & Li: The Battle at Dai[/i]. It might feel like I’ve revealed too much, but honestly, this story still needs much enrichment and detail.[/p]
